title: Jaishankar Calls US a 'Lonelier Power', Urges Middle Path Between America and China
excerpt: At the Munich Leaders Meeting, the external affairs minister said Washington had deliberately drifted, China is rising sharply, and middle powers must navigate between them with a 'Goldilocks' balance.
body:
• External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, speaking at the Munich Leaders Meeting on Oct. 4, described a world order shaped by two forces: the "radical repositioning" of the United States and the rise of China.
  • He called for a "Goldilocks scenario" in US-China rivalry — "You don't want it to be too hot; you don't want it to be too good; you want it somewhere in between."
  • His prescription for middle powers: self-reliance, strategic hedging and pragmatic, agenda-based partnerships instead of rigid alliances.
  • He also defended India's ties with Russia, recalling that Moscow "stood by us" when India's security and territorial integrity were under threat.

External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar has given the bluntest recent account of how New Delhi reads the changing global order: a United States that has "deliberately become a lonelier power," a rising China locked in "very sharp competition" with it, and a world where leverage itself has become a weapon.

Speaking at the Munich Leaders Meeting on Oct. 4, Jaishankar argued that the international landscape is now defined by two primary forces. The first, he said, is Washington's radical repositioning.

"The landscape today is primarily marked by a radical repositioning of the United States... a posture of choice [where] it has deliberately become a lonelier power."

— S. Jaishankar, External Affairs Minister of India

The second feature, he said, is "of course, the rise of China" — a country that sees itself as unique, "and in many ways, also the reality. And we are looking at very sharp competition." That competition, he argued, has produced the "weaponisation of leverage": in an interdependent world of supply chains, markets and production, "who leverages what" decides who holds the upper hand.

A Goldilocks scenario

Jaishankar's answer to the US-China friction was a middle-path metaphor. "We are looking at what is often called the Goldilocks scenario," he said.

https://x.com/DrSJaishankar/status/2106695621004656739

"You don't want it to be too hot; you don't want it to be too good; you want it somewhere in between."

— S. Jaishankar, External Affairs Minister of India

His counsel to emerging and middle powers was to navigate the fractured order through self-reliance, strategic hedging and pragmatic partnerships rather than rigid alliances — diversifying and de-risking their economies, security and supply chains. "The days when you have to have an identity of views or a very strong congruence of interest, I think that's too high a bar today," he said. "If you have enough touch points, that is good enough for countries to work together." Slowly, he argued, "a new architecture is coming into place" as middle powers build agenda-based cooperation.

Russia, Ukraine and the balancing act

Jaishankar also used the platform to defend India's continuing engagement with Russia, a subject of persistent Western unease. "India and Russia have historically very good relations, particularly since the 1950s. That history is not forgotten," he said, recalling that the Soviet Union "stood by us in many ways when our security, when our territorial integrity was under threat," at a time when much of the world backed a military regime next to India. The relationship, he said, has since widened into a substantial economic one — trade, investment, energy and resources — alongside military, nuclear and space cooperation.

On Ukraine, he detailed India's outreach to both Kyiv and Moscow, noting Prime Minister Narendra Modi's wide-ranging talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Bishkek on Aug. 31, where Modi pressed that the "endless war must now give way to end of war."

What it means for the diaspora

For the Indian diaspora, this is the clearest articulation of the foreign-policy environment they live inside: Indians in the United States, in the Gulf, in Europe and in East Asia all stand to be affected by how India positions itself between a repositioning America and an assertive China. The "Goldilocks" framing — not too close to Washington, not too hostile to Beijing, leverage built through self-reliance — signals that New Delhi's balancing act, and the diplomacy, trade and technology partnerships it produces, will continue to define the economic and political weather for the diaspora for years.

What's next

Jaishankar's remarks set the tone for India's diplomatic calendar into the new year, with the framework of diversified partnerships and "reasonable convergence" likely to feature at every major summit. Watch for how the doctrine translates into concrete agreements — on supply chains, defence, critical minerals and technology — and for how Washington and Beijing respond to being told, in effect, that the middle powers are done choosing sides.
